quests.instruction: Which link has a nasal sound meeting a vowel?
quests.textToSpeak: I've had a sharp pain in my lower back since Monday
quests.hint: Look for a noun that ends in a hum.
quests.explanation: The /n/ of 'pain' runs into the /ɪ/ of 'in', so 'pain in my lower back' starts as one chunk. 'Had a' is the other link, through /d/.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Find the link carried by a 'th' sound
quests.textToSpeak: does it hurt more when you breathe in or out
quests.hint: A voiced 'th' meets a vowel. Find it.
quests.explanation: 'Breathe' ends in /ð/ (the e is silent), and the voiced 'th' flows into 'in'. 'In or' and 'or out' follow, so the sentence is a chain. Clinicians say it quickly, so the link is easy to miss.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (/θ/ and /ð/): The 'th' sounds at the end of a word stay in the airflow and connect to a following vowel instead of stopping.

quests.instruction: Find the final link
quests.textToSpeak: take two tablets and call us if it gets any worse
quests.hint: Several boundaries link, but the question wants the one nearest the final word.
quests.explanation: The /ts/ of 'gets' lands on the /e/ of 'any', ending the instruction. 'Tablets and', 'call us' and 'us if' come earlier. The end of a medical instruction is said slowly for clarity, yet the link still holds.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Which pair is joined by a nasal sound?
quests.textToSpeak: the landlord says the heating is part of the rent
quests.hint: One boundary keeps the voice running without any burst or hiss. Where?
quests.explanation: Landlord talk is said quickly, so the nasal link is easiest to catch. The /ŋ/ of 'heating' hums into the /ɪ/ of 'is', and 'part of' links through /t/.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Which pair is joined by a 'ch' or 'j' sound?
quests.textToSpeak: we need to arrange a viewing at the earliest opportunity
quests.hint: Which boundary starts with a soft burst and a hiss, then a vowel?
quests.explanation: 'Arrange' ends in /dʒ/, which is released straight into the weak /ə/ of 'a'. 'Viewing at', 'earliest opportunity' and 'the earliest' link other ways. A formal request keeps its flow.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (affricates): The 'ch' sound /tʃ/ and the 'j' sound /dʒ/ at the end of a word are released directly into the next vowel instead of being cut off.

quests.instruction: Find the link where a word ending in two consonants joins a vowel
quests.textToSpeak: is the flat available from the first of next month
quests.hint: Say each word alone: one ends in a cluster. In the sentence, the cluster is carried into the next vowel.
quests.explanation: Dates in speech are compressed. The /st/ of 'first' is carried into the weak /əv/ of 'of', and 'flat available' links through a single /t/.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Find the link where a written r returns before a vowel
quests.textToSpeak: I'd like to transfer an amount from my savings account
quests.hint: Check the spelling: which word ends in r or re and is followed by a vowel?
quests.explanation: 'Transfer' ends in a written r, so the /r/ appears before the weak /ən/ of 'an' (always in rhotic accents). 'An amount' and 'savings account' link through other sounds.
quests.flowRule: Linking /r/ (accent-dependent): In rhotic accents (most of North America, Scotland, Ireland) a word-final r is always pronounced, so it simply connects to a following vowel. In non-rhotic accents (for example most of England, Australia, New Zealand) the r is silent before a consonant or a pause but usually returns before a vowel, as in 'far away'. Either way, the two words connect.

quests.instruction: Find the link carried by the sound /l/
quests.textToSpeak: please fill in the form and attach your passport
quests.hint: Say each word alone: one ends in /l/. Does a vowel follow it in the sentence?
quests.explanation: The dark /l/ of 'fill' stays on the tongue as the vowel of 'in' begins. 'Form and' and 'and attach' follow, so the instruction is delivered as a chain.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (/l/): A word-final /l/ stays voiced and slides into the vowel of the next word, so the two words sound like one continuous stretch.

quests.instruction: Find the link that keeps a past-tense -ed audible
quests.textToSpeak: your application was received on the third of March
quests.hint: Find the -ed verb and check whether a vowel follows it.
quests.explanation: Dates are spoken in one flow, and the tense stays audible: the /d/ of 'received' lands on the vowel of 'on'. 'Your application' and 'third of' link through other sounds.
quests.flowRule: Past-tense endings link too: A final -ed (/t/ or /d/) joins a following vowel, which also keeps the past-tense signal audible.

quests.instruction: Find the first place where one word runs into the next
quests.textToSpeak: I returned the item last week but I haven't had a refund
quests.hint: Several boundaries link, but only one comes first. Which?
quests.explanation: A complaint is delivered as one flow: the /t/ of 'but' lands on the /aɪ/ of 'I'. 'Had a' follows through /d/. The first link is the part of the sentence that carries the contrast.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Which connection comes first in this sentence?
quests.textToSpeak: the parcel tracking says it was delivered but nothing has arrived
quests.hint: Start at the left and stop at the first consonant-to-vowel join.
quests.explanation: The /z/ of 'says' runs into the /ɪ/ of 'it', so the report of the tracking message starts as one chunk. The remaining links, such as 'has arrived', carry on the flow.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Find the link that slides through a 'w' sound
quests.textToSpeak: please look into it then let me know by tomorrow
quests.hint: Say the pair slowly and notice if a 'w' appears: 'go-wup', 'who-wis'. Where?
quests.explanation: The rounded /uː/ of 'into' slides into the /ɪ/ of 'it' with a faint /w/. 'Look into' is a consonant-to-vowel link. A polite request to 'look into it' is said fast.
quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /w/ glide: After vowels made with rounded lips (/uː/, /əʊ/, /aʊ/), many speakers slide through a light /w/ before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.instruction: Which pair could be misheard as different words because the link hides the gap?
quests.textToSpeak: we put some ice in the drinks
quests.hint: Which pair could be misheard if the /m/ is taken as the start of the next word?
quests.explanation: 'Some ice' and 'some mice' sound almost identical because the /m/ of 'some' links into the vowel and blurs the boundary. Context, here the drinks, tells you it must be ice.
quests.flowRule: Misleading segmentation: The same stream of sounds can be split into different words (an aim / a name, at all / a tall). Linking removes the clear gaps that spelling shows, so context, grammar and stress decide which words were meant.

quests.instruction: Which link may get an extra /r/ in some accents, even though no r is written?
quests.textToSpeak: the extra option is cheaper
quests.hint: A word ending in a weak vowel meets a vowel.
quests.explanation: Some non-rhotic speakers say 'extrar option' with an /r/ that is not in the spelling; others glide or pause slightly. It is accent-dependent and worth recognising, even if you never produce it.
quests.flowRule: Intrusive /r/ (accent-dependent): In some non-rhotic accents speakers add an /r/ between a word ending in /ə/, /ɑː/ or /ɔː/ and a following vowel even when no r is written (idea of sounds like 'idear of'). It is common in those accents and absent in others, so it is useful to recognise but not something you need to produce.

quests.instruction: Which pair seems to join two vowels in spelling but does not in sound?
quests.textToSpeak: I paid a utility bill online
quests.hint: Say each vowel-letter word on its own and listen to its first sound. One starts with a consonant sound.
quests.explanation: 'Utility' begins with /j/, so nothing links between 'a' and 'utility'. The real links in this sentence are 'paid a' and 'bill online'.
quests.flowRule: Sound, not spelling (glides): Spelling can suggest a vowel-to-vowel link where there is none. 'One' begins with /w/ and 'unique' with /j/, so they are consonant sounds. Check the first sound of a word, not its first letter.

quests.instruction: Which pair is joined by a 'th' sound?
quests.textToSpeak: heavy rain is expected across the north and east of the country
quests.hint: A breathy 'th' ends a compass word. Which pair?
quests.explanation: The /θ/ of 'north' flows into the weak /ən/ of 'and', so a weather forecast keeps its pace. 'East of' and 'rain is' link through other sounds.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (/θ/ and /ð/): The 'th' sounds at the end of a word stay in the airflow and connect to a following vowel instead of stopping.

quests.instruction: Which link do you hear first?
quests.textToSpeak: trains are running about ten minutes late due to an earlier fault
quests.hint: Read left to right and take the earliest link.
quests.explanation: The /z/ of 'trains' lands on the weak vowel of 'are', so 'trains are' is one unit. Announcements are paced for clarity, but the first link still joins.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Find the link where a word ending in three consonants joins a vowel
quests.textToSpeak: the minister announced a new policy on housing and education
quests.hint: Look for a word ending in three consonants.
quests.explanation: News reports keep the cluster rather than dropping it. The /nst/ of 'announced' hands its /t/ to the weak /ə/ of 'a', so the link still holds.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Spot the vowel-to-vowel link that takes a 'y' glide
quests.textToSpeak: I'm struggling to find enough time for all of my assignments
quests.hint: Say the pair slowly and notice if a 'y' appears: 'see-yit', 'say-yit'. Where?
quests.explanation: 'My' ends in /aɪ/ and 'assignments' begins with the weak /ə/, so a light /j/ slips between them. 'Find enough' links through /d/. Students describing workloads speak quickly.
quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /j/ glide: After vowels made with the tongue high and forward (/iː/, /eɪ/, /aɪ/, /ɔɪ/), many speakers slide through a light /j/ ('y') before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.instruction: Which link carries a linking /r/?
quests.textToSpeak: could we go through the feedback together at some point
quests.hint: Look for a word ending in -er before a vowel.
quests.explanation: 'Together' ends in a written r, which links into the weak /ət/ of 'at'. It is the only link in the sentence, so a speaker who pauses after 'together' sounds as if a new thought is starting.
quests.flowRule: Linking /r/ (accent-dependent): In rhotic accents (most of North America, Scotland, Ireland) a word-final r is always pronounced, so it simply connects to a following vowel. In non-rhotic accents (for example most of England, Australia, New Zealand) the r is silent before a consonant or a pause but usually returns before a vowel, as in 'far away'. Either way, the two words connect.

quests.instruction: Which pair is joined by an -ed ending?
quests.textToSpeak: my tutor mentioned it before the seminar
quests.hint: Find a verb in the past tense. Its ending is a /t/ or /d/ that attaches to the next word.
quests.explanation: Without the /d/ of 'mentioned', the verb would sound like present tense, so it matters that it lands on the vowel of 'it'. 'Tutor mentioned' does not link, because a weak vowel meets /m/.
quests.flowRule: Past-tense endings link too: A final -ed (/t/ or /d/) joins a following vowel, which also keeps the past-tense signal audible.

quests.instruction: Which link carries the past-tense ending?
quests.textToSpeak: the neighbors complained about the noise at around midnight
quests.hint: Which verb ends in a past-tense -ed that you might be tempted to drop?
quests.explanation: People describing a complaint say it at speed, and the tense survives: the /d/ of 'complained' lands on the weak /ə/ of 'about'. 'Noise at' and 'at around' link through other sounds.
quests.flowRule: Past-tense endings link too: A final -ed (/t/ or /d/) joins a following vowel, which also keeps the past-tense signal audible.

quests.instruction: Which link has a light /j/ ('y') glide between two vowels?
quests.textToSpeak: there's a community meeting on Thursday evening at the library
quests.hint: The first vowel of the link finishes with the tongue high and forward. Which pair?
quests.explanation: 'Thursday' ends in /eɪ/ and 'evening' begins with /iː/, so a light /j/ eases the move. Event announcements are said clearly, but the glide is usually there.
quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /j/ glide: After vowels made with the tongue high and forward (/iː/, /eɪ/, /aɪ/, /ɔɪ/), many speakers slide through a light /j/ ('y') before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.instruction: Which link carries a consonant cluster?
quests.textToSpeak: someone has left a bag of rubbish outside our door
quests.hint: A cluster makes this link harder to hear. Which boundary has one?
quests.explanation: The cluster is the link that stands out here: the /ft/ of 'left' hands its /t/ to the weak /ə/ of 'a'. 'Bag of' and 'outside our' link through single consonants.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Which pair changes into a 'ch', 'j' or 'sh' sound when said quickly?
quests.textToSpeak: I really appreciate the effort you put into this project
quests.hint: Find the pair where the two sounds at the join become one.
quests.explanation: 'Effort you' becomes 'effortcha' as /t/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/. Managers giving praise often use this informal form, though a careful speaker may not.
quests.flowRule: Yod-coalescence (informal speech): When a word ending in /t/, /d/, /s/ or /z/ is followed by 'you' or 'your', the two sounds often merge into one: /t/+/j/ becomes /tʃ/ ('got you' sounds like 'gotcha'), /d/+/j/ becomes /dʒ/ ('did you' like 'didja'), /s/+/j/ becomes /ʃ/ and /z/+/j/ becomes /ʒ/. This is a normal informal reduction, not a mistake, and careful speakers may keep the sounds apart.

quests.instruction: Find the link that runs on a hum (m, n or ng)
quests.textToSpeak: one area to improve is how we communicate under pressure
quests.hint: In which pair does the first word end with your mouth closed or your tongue tip up, with sound still flowing?
quests.explanation: The /n/ of 'one' runs into the vowel of 'area', so 'one area' is heard as a unit. 'Communicate under' links through /t/. Feedback conversations tend to be said in a thoughtful, steady tone.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Find the link where a held sound like s, z, f or v flows into a vowel
quests.textToSpeak: you handled that difficult call calmly and the client was impressed
quests.hint: Which link is carried by a buzz?
quests.explanation: The /z/ of 'was' runs into the /ɪ/ of 'impressed', so the praise ends as one flowing phrase. 'Calmly and' is a vowel-to-vowel link, which is a separate matter.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (continuous sounds): Sounds you can hold, such as /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/ and /ʃ/, glide directly into a following vowel without restarting.

quests.instruction: Which link has a nasal sound meeting a vowel?
quests.textToSpeak: she's an excellent speaker and always arrives well prepared
quests.hint: Say the sentence with your nose pinched. Which boundary suddenly sounds blocked?
quests.explanation: The /n/ of 'an' hums into the /ɛ/ of 'excellent'. 'She's an', 'and always' and 'always arrives' link through other sounds. A glowing reference is said smoothly.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Find the link into a word whose h you do not pronounce
quests.textToSpeak: he received an honorary degree last year
quests.hint: Look for a word whose first letter is silent.
quests.explanation: The h of 'honorary' is silent in this word, so it begins with a vowel and takes 'an'. The /n/ links straight in. 'Received an' links through /d/ as well.
quests.flowRule: Silent 'h': In words like 'hour', 'honest' and 'honour' the written h is not pronounced, so the word begins with a vowel sound and links to the word before it (and takes 'an', not 'a').

quests.instruction: Find the link carried by a 'ch' or 'j' sound
quests.textToSpeak: we must have missed each other at the station
quests.hint: A 'ch' or 'j' sound ends one word. What does it meet?
quests.explanation: The 'ch' of 'each' is released into the weak /ʌ/ of 'other', so the pair sounds like one word. 'Missed each' and 'other at' link through other sounds, so the sentence is a chain.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (affricates): The 'ch' sound /tʃ/ and the 'j' sound /dʒ/ at the end of a word are released directly into the next vowel instead of being cut off.
